title: Reproductive Gross and Microscopic Anatomy
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the cells and tissue zones of the testis, male ducts, female tract, ovary, breast, and prostate that board questions most often show on a slide or describe in a case. For each site you will learn what the cells look like, what they make, which hormone controls them, and which disease begins there. The organizing idea is that structure predicts disease: the blood-testis barrier explains antisperm antibodies, the transformation zone explains where cervical dysplasia starts, the two-layer breast duct separates in situ from invasive carcinoma, and prostate zone position explains why hyperplasia obstructs urine flow early while carcinoma is often silent.
prerequisites: Epithelial classification (simple, stratified, pseudostratified; squamous, cuboidal, columnar) and apical specializations such as cilia and stereocilia
Cell junctions, especially tight junctions and gap junctions
Hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis: GnRH, LH, FSH, and negative feedback
Steroid synthesis from cholesterol, including aromatase and 5-alpha-reductase (RE-8)
Meiosis and the timing of meiotic arrest in oocytes and spermatocytes (RE-3)

sections.title: Sertoli cells and Leydig cells of the testis

blocks.text: The testis has two working compartments. The seminiferous tubules make sperm, and the interstitium between them makes testosterone. Each tubule is lined by seminiferous epithelium (germ cells plus supporting Sertoli cells) on a basement membrane, ringed by contractile peritubular myoid cells that move immotile sperm toward the rete testis.
Sertoli cells: support, barrier, and FSH response

Sertoli cells are tall columnar cells that span the full height of the epithelium, from basement membrane to lumen. On a slide they are recognized by a pale, oval or triangular, often folded nucleus with a prominent nucleolus, sitting near the basement membrane, and by indistinct cell borders. Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells, just above the spermatogonia, form the blood-testis barrier. It divides the epithelium into a basal compartment, open to substances from the interstitial capillaries, and an adluminal compartment that only material crossing Sertoli cells can enter. Primary spermatocytes move across the barrier early in meiosis, so every meiotic and haploid cell, which carries antigens that appeared long after immune tolerance was established, is sequestered from immune cells.

Sertoli cells carry the FSH receptors and the androgen receptors that drive spermatogenesis; germ cells themselves lack androgen receptors and depend on Sertoli cells to relay the testosterone signal. In response, Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein, which holds intratubular testosterone far above the serum level, and inhibin B, which feeds back on the pituitary to lower FSH. They also secrete tubular fluid, phagocytose the residual cytoplasm shed by maturing spermatids, aromatize some testosterone to estradiol, and in the fetus secrete anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH).
Leydig cells: testosterone under LH

Leydig (interstitial) cells lie in clusters in the loose connective tissue between tubules, beside capillaries into which they secrete. They are polygonal with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, lipid droplets, round nuclei, and, in humans, rod-shaped Reinke crystals. Their abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with tubular cristae mark them as steroid-producing cells. LH binds Leydig cell receptors, raises cAMP, and increases cholesterol transport into mitochondria by steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR), the rate-limiting step in testosterone synthesis.

blocks.title: Split feedback of the testis
steps: LH drives Leydig testosterone; FSH drives Sertoli function
blocks.caption: Leydig cell output controls LH and Sertoli cell output controls FSH, so a lab pattern can localize damage to one cell type.

blocks.text: This split explains classic patterns. Spermatogenesis needs a scrotal temperature about 2 to 3 °C (about 4 to 5 °F) below core. In an undescended testis, heat damages germ and Sertoli cells, so sperm count and inhibin B fall and FSH rises, while Leydig cells keep testosterone near normal. When the barrier is breached by trauma, orchitis, or vasectomy, exposed sperm antigens can provoke antisperm antibodies.

blocks.predict: A man has a selective rise in serum FSH with normal LH and testosterone. Which testicular cell is failing?
blocks.explain: The Sertoli cell and its germ cells. Less inhibin B removes the brake on FSH, while intact Leydig cells keep testosterone, and therefore LH, normal.

sections.title: The path of sperm from tubule to urethra

blocks.text: Sperm released into the tubule lumen are immotile and cannot yet fertilize. The duct system carries them through sites of maturation, storage, and propulsion, and each segment's lining fits its job. The sequence is fixed, so obstruction at any point stops sperm from reaching the ejaculate even though the testis keeps working.

blocks.title: Path of sperm
steps: Rete testis in the mediastinum testis
blocks.caption: Sperm pass from the testis through the excurrent ducts and exit by the three parts of the male urethra.

blocks.title: Lining and role of each segment
rows: Alternating ciliated columnar and nonciliated cuboidal cells (scalloped lumen)
Absorb most tubular fluid; cilia move sperm to the epididymal head
Absorption, maturation, storage in the tail
Pseudostratified columnar with stereocilia; thick three-layer smooth muscle
Passes through the external urethral sphincter
Pseudostratified or stratified columnar; stratified squamous at the navicular fossa
blocks.caption: Epithelium changes from absorptive and ciliated in the testis outflow to muscular conduits and then urethral linings.

blocks.text: The epididymis is a single, tightly coiled duct several meters long. Its principal cells absorb fluid through stereocilia, which concentrates sperm, and secrete proteins that remodel the sperm membrane. During several days of transit sperm acquire forward motility and the ability to bind the zona pellucida, and they are stored in the tail. Final activation, called capacitation, occurs later in the female tract.

The ductus deferens begins at the epididymal tail, ascends in the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal from the superficial to the deep inguinal ring, and descends on the lateral pelvic wall. It crosses superior to the ureter, widens into the ampulla behind the bladder, and joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct. Each ejaculatory duct traverses the prostate and opens on the seminal colliculus in the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra. During emission, sympathetic fibers contract the ductal smooth muscle; during ejaculation, rhythmic contraction of the bulbospongiosus expels semen.

Most semen volume does not come from the testis. Seminal vesicles contribute the largest share, an alkaline, fructose-rich fluid, and the prostate adds a thin, slightly acidic fluid with citrate, zinc, and PSA. Ductal obstruction therefore produces a characteristic pattern: azoospermia with normal testosterone, LH, and FSH. In congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, associated with CFTR mutations, the seminal vesicles are usually also abnormal, so the ejaculate is low in volume, acidic, and lacks fructose.

blocks.title: Worked example: obstructive or testicular azoospermia?
blocks.text: Two men have no sperm in the ejaculate. Man A has normal testosterone, LH, and FSH, normal testis size, and low semen volume with low fructose. Man B has small testes, high FSH, low inhibin B, and normal semen volume. In A the testes are working, because normal FSH means inhibin B is normal, so sperm are made but blocked; low volume and fructose place the block at the ejaculatory ducts or at absent vasa and seminal vesicles. In B the Sertoli and germ cell compartment has failed, so inhibin B falls and FSH rises; the ducts are patent, but nothing is entering them. The hormone pattern localizes the problem.

sections.title: Epithelia of the female tract and the cervical transformation zone

blocks.text: The female tract changes its lining along its length to match local demands. Upper segments transport gametes and support implantation, so they are lined by simple columnar epithelium with cilia or glands. Lower segments face friction during intercourse and childbirth, so they are lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The meeting point of these two epithelia on the cervix is the most important site of epithelial disease in the tract.

Simple columnar surface with simple tubular glands in cellular stroma
Functional layer sheds monthly; basal layer regenerates it
Simple columnar mucus-secreting cells lining branched crypts
Mucus changes with the cycle; blocked crypts form Nabothian cysts
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous, glycogen-rich; no glands
Lactobacilli ferment glycogen breakdown products to lactic acid (pH about 3.8 to 4.5)
blocks.caption: Columnar linings serve transport and secretion; squamous linings resist abrasion.

blocks.text: The uterine tube has a muscular wall and a mucosa that is most elaborately folded in the ampulla, the usual site of fertilization. Estrogen increases ciliation and secretory activity. Because ciliary beating, aided by peristalsis, moves the embryo toward the uterus, scarring and loss of cilia after salpingitis delay transport and raise the risk of tubal ectopic pregnancy.

The endometrium has a functional layer, supplied by spiral arteries and shed at menstruation, and a basal layer, supplied by straight arteries and retained to regenerate the next functional layer. In the proliferative phase, estrogen produces straight, narrow glands with mitoses; in the secretory phase, progesterone produces coiled glands with glycogen vacuoles and an edematous stroma. Destruction of the basal layer, as by aggressive curettage, prevents regeneration.
The transformation zone

The squamocolumnar junction is where endocervical columnar epithelium meets ectocervical squamous epithelium. Its position moves. At puberty, in pregnancy, and with estrogen exposure, the cervix enlarges and everts, exposing columnar epithelium on the ectocervix (ectropion). In the acidic vagina, subcolumnar reserve cells undergo squamous metaplasia, and a new junction forms closer to the os. The band between the original and the new junction is the transformation zone. After menopause the junction recedes into the endocervical canal, which is why sampling must reach into the canal in older women.

blocks.title: From transformation zone to cervical dysplasia
steps: Eversion exposes columnar epithelium to acidic vaginal pH
High-risk HPV enters immature metaplastic basal cells
E6 promotes p53 degradation; E7 inactivates Rb
Cell-cycle checkpoints are lost; mutations accumulate
Dysplasia (CIN) begins in the transformation zone
blocks.caption: Actively dividing metaplastic cells are the most vulnerable target for high-risk HPV types such as 16 and 18.

blocks.text: Immature metaplastic cells divide actively, and HPV reaches the basal layer through microabrasions, so this zone is where nearly all cervical squamous dysplasia and carcinoma arise. Endocervical adenocarcinoma also arises near the junction from glandular cells. Cytologic and HPV screening sample the transformation zone for this reason.

blocks.predict: Why might a cervical sample from a 65-year-old miss dysplasia if it scrapes only the ectocervix?
blocks.explain: After menopause the squamocolumnar junction and transformation zone retract into the endocervical canal, so an ectocervical sample may contain only mature squamous cells.

sections.title: Ovarian follicles and the corpus luteum

blocks.text: The ovary has a cortex of follicles in cellular stroma and a vascular medulla, covered by simple cuboidal surface epithelium. Every follicle surrounds a primary oocyte arrested in the diplotene stage of prophase I, an arrest that can last from fetal life to menopause. Follicle stages are named by changes in the layers around that oocyte: granulosa cells inside the follicular basement membrane, and theca cells that condense from stroma outside it.

blocks.title: Follicle stages
rows: Primary oocyte enlarges; zona pellucida forms
Cuboidal, first one layer then several
Stromal cells begin to organize as theca
Many layers with fluid spaces merging into an antrum
Theca interna (vascular, steroid-making) and theca externa (fibrous)
Completes meiosis I after the LH surge; secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II
Oocyte on the cumulus oophorus, ringed by corona radiata
Large antrum; follicle about 2 cm, bulging at the surface
Smaller, darker theca lutein cells at the periphery; progesterone and estradiol
blocks.caption: Each stage adds granulosa layers, then fluid, then a theca; luteinization converts both layers into a progesterone-secreting gland.

blocks.text: In the primary follicle the oocyte and granulosa cells secrete the zona pellucida, a glycoprotein coat that later binds sperm. Granulosa cell processes cross the zona and connect to the oocyte by gap junctions, which deliver nutrients and keep the oocyte arrested. Granulosa cells have no blood vessels, because capillaries stop at the basement membrane in the theca interna. Most follicles never ovulate; they undergo atresia, with apoptosis of granulosa cells and collapse of the oocyte.

Estradiol synthesis requires both cell types, because each lacks an enzyme the other has. Theca interna cells have LH receptors and 17-alpha-hydroxylase activity (CYP17) and make androgens, but they lack aromatase. Granulosa cells lack CYP17 and cannot make androgens, but FSH induces aromatase in them.

blocks.title: Two-cell, two-gonadotropin estradiol synthesis
steps: Theca cells convert cholesterol to androstenedione
Androgen diffuses across the basement membrane
FSH induces aromatase in granulosa cells
Granulosa cells aromatize the androgen to estrogen
Estradiol enters follicular fluid and blood
blocks.caption: Theca supplies the androgen substrate and granulosa supplies aromatase; neither alone makes much estradiol.

blocks.text: After ovulation the basement membrane breaks down, capillaries invade the former granulosa layer, and LH luteinizes both cell types. The new blood supply delivers LDL cholesterol, which allows high-volume progesterone output. Granulosa lutein cells, the larger and paler majority, make progesterone and, with aromatase, estradiol; theca lutein cells make androgens and progesterone. Without hCG the corpus luteum regresses after about 14 days into the corpus albicans, a white collagen scar. In pregnancy, hCG from the trophoblast maintains it until placental progesterone takes over at about 7 to 9 weeks.

Recognizing these cells explains several ovarian lesions. Granulosa cell tumors secrete estrogen and may show small rosettes around eosinophilic material (Call-Exner bodies). In polycystic ovary syndrome, multiple small antral follicles and hyperplastic theca produce excess androgen. A follicular cyst is an unruptured follicle; a corpus luteum cyst can bleed.

sections.title: The terminal duct lobular unit of the breast

blocks.text: The adult breast is a modified apocrine sweat gland made of about 15 to 20 lobes embedded in fat and dense fibrous stroma. Each lobe drains through a lactiferous duct that widens into a lactiferous sinus beneath the nipple. Moving away from the nipple, ducts branch into segmental and subsegmental ducts and end in terminal ducts, each of which feeds a lobule of small blind-ended ductules called acini.

The terminal duct and its lobule, together with the loose, hormonally responsive intralobular stroma around the acini, form the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU). This is the secretory unit of the breast and the unit that responds to each menstrual cycle, to pregnancy, and to menopause. The surrounding interlobular stroma is denser and less cellular.
Two cell layers

Every duct and acinus, from the large ducts to the acini, is lined by two cell layers on a basement membrane. The inner luminal cells are cuboidal to columnar; a subset expresses estrogen and progesterone receptors, and in lactation these cells secrete milk proteins and lipid. The outer myoepithelial cells are contractile and squeeze milk toward the nipple in response to oxytocin. They express smooth muscle actin, calponin, and the nuclear protein p63, markers pathologists stain for, and they help maintain the basement membrane.

rows: Ductal and lobular carcinoma in situ
Invasive ductal (no special type) and lobular carcinoma
Intralobular stroma of the TDLU, with entrapped ducts
Usually large ducts beneath the nipple (solitary papilloma)
Proliferating acini and stroma of the TDLU
Present, which separates it from carcinoma
blocks.caption: The cell layer of origin and the fate of the myoepithelial layer classify most breast lesions.

blocks.text: Most breast carcinomas, both ductal and lobular, arise from luminal cells of the TDLU. The names ductal and lobular describe the growth pattern and cell biology (lobular carcinoma lacks E-cadherin), not the anatomic site. Fibroadenoma arises from the specialized intralobular stroma, so it is biphasic: proliferating stroma with compressed but normal two-layered ducts. It is common in young women because the intralobular stroma is hormone responsive. The main exception is solitary intraductal papilloma, which usually arises in the large ducts beneath the nipple.

The myoepithelial layer is the key to invasion. While neoplastic luminal cells stay inside the basement membrane, myoepithelial cells still surround them and the lesion is in situ. Invasive carcinoma has crossed the basement membrane into stroma with no myoepithelial rim. Benign mimics such as sclerosing adenosis keep the layer even when the glands look crowded and distorted.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the myoepithelial stain
blocks.text: A breast biopsy shows crowded, angulated glands in dense stroma. To decide whether they are invasive, the pathologist stains for p63 and smooth muscle myosin, which mark myoepithelial cells. If each gland is ringed by brown p63-positive nuclei, the two-layer structure is intact and the basement membrane has not been breached, which fits sclerosing adenosis or an in situ lesion. If the glands have no outer ring of p63-positive nuclei, epithelial cells have escaped the basement membrane into stroma, which is invasive carcinoma. The same structural logic applies to prostate basal cells.

The prostate surrounds the first part of the urethra below the bladder neck. Its glands are tubuloalveolar, with luminal secretory cells over a layer of flat basal cells, embedded in fibromuscular stroma. The secretory cells make the prostatic component of semen, including PSA and acid phosphatase, and their lumens may contain lamellated corpora amylacea. Lobes such as the median lobe are still used clinically, but pathology and imaging use zones, because each zone has a characteristic disease.

blocks.title: Prostate zones
rows: Posterior, lateral, and apical; lies against the rectum
Cone around the ejaculatory ducts at the base
Two small lobes around the proximal prostatic urethra
blocks.caption: Zone position relative to the urethra and rectum determines what a lesion does and how it is found.

blocks.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is nodular hyperplasia of glands and stroma arising in the transition zone and the periurethral tissue. Its driver is dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Stromal cells express type 2 5-alpha-reductase, convert testosterone to DHT, and DHT acting on androgen receptors in stromal and epithelial cells increases growth factor production. Because the transition zone wraps the urethra, even modest growth compresses it. Increased smooth muscle tone in the hyperplastic stroma, under alpha-1 adrenergic control, adds a dynamic component to obstruction.

blocks.title: From DHT to urinary obstruction in BPH
steps: Transition zone nodules of stroma and glands enlarge
Prostatic urethra is compressed; stromal smooth muscle tone adds
Hesitancy, weak stream, retention; bladder wall hypertrophies
blocks.caption: Hyperplasia in the transition zone narrows the urethra, and the bladder works harder to empty against it.

blocks.text: Obstruction explains the manifestations. The bladder detrusor hypertrophies and becomes trabeculated, diverticula form, residual urine predisposes to infection and stones, and sustained retention can cause hydronephrosis. Gland size on rectal exam correlates poorly with symptoms, because a small amount of periurethral growth can obstruct. BPH arises in a different zone from most carcinomas and is not considered a precursor of cancer.

Prostatic adenocarcinoma arises mostly in the peripheral zone, often multifocally, with high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia as its precursor. Because the peripheral zone lies against the rectum and away from the urethra, carcinoma is often found as a firm or hard nodule on rectal exam and causes urinary symptoms only when advanced. Histologically, malignant glands lack the basal cell layer, which pathologists confirm with basal cell stains such as p63 and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin, and they often overexpress AMACR. PSA rises in both BPH and carcinoma, so it reflects prostate tissue rather than cancer specifically.

blocks.predict: Why can a large peripheral zone carcinoma be silent while a small transition zone nodule causes urinary retention?
blocks.explain: The transition zone surrounds the urethra, so small growth compresses it; the peripheral zone is posterior and lateral, so a tumor there must grow large or invade before it narrows the urethra.

integration.text: Across this chapter, a single structural fact explains a disease pattern. Tight junctions between Sertoli cells sequester antigens that arose after tolerance was established, so trauma, mumps orchitis, or vasectomy can produce antisperm antibodies. Embryology sets the plan: Sertoli cell AMH removes the Mullerian ducts and Leydig cell testosterone preserves the Wolffian ducts that become the epididymis, ductus deferens, and seminal vesicles. Biochemistry divides labor between cells, with theca androgens and granulosa aromatase in the ovary and stromal 5-alpha-reductase driving prostatic growth.

Pathology follows the cell layer. Metaplastic cells at the cervical transformation zone are the target of high-risk HPV, and the oncoproteins E6 and E7 link microbiology to loss of p53 and Rb control. In breast and prostate, the outer cell layer (myoepithelial or basal) separates benign and in situ lesions from invasive carcinoma. Zone position explains symptoms in the prostate. These rules have limits: some carcinomas arise outside the expected zone, epithelial boundaries shift with age and hormones, and immunostains support but do not replace the whole histologic picture.

summary: Sertoli cells span the seminiferous epithelium, form the blood-testis barrier with tight junctions, respond to FSH, and secrete androgen-binding protein, inhibin B, and fetal AMH.
Leydig cells in the interstitium respond to LH and make testosterone; they are eosinophilic, lipid-rich, and may contain Reinke crystals.
Inhibin B selectively suppresses FSH and testosterone suppresses LH, so a selective FSH rise points to Sertoli and germ cell failure.
Sperm travel through seminiferous tubules, straight tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, and the prostatic, membranous, and spongy urethra.
Ductal obstruction gives azoospermia with normal hormones; absent vasa and seminal vesicles give low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative semen.
The uterine tube is ciliated simple columnar, the endometrium and endocervix are simple columnar, and the ectocervix and vagina are nonkeratinized stratified squamous.
The transformation zone is metaplastic epithelium between the old and new squamocolumnar junctions, where HPV-driven dysplasia begins; it moves into the canal after menopause.
Follicles progress from flat to cuboidal to multilayered granulosa, then antrum formation; theca interna makes androgens under LH, and granulosa aromatizes them under FSH.
Most breast carcinomas and fibroadenomas arise in the TDLU, carcinoma from luminal epithelium and fibroadenoma from intralobular stroma; loss of myoepithelial cells marks invasion.
BPH arises in the transition zone around the urethra and obstructs early; most prostate carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, are palpable, and lack basal cells.
